note: Started 2026-08-16. NOT A COMPLETE AUDIT — this began as the worklist, with two bibliographic checks completed and every substantive verdict 'unchecked'. One substantive verdict has since been settled from the primary source: kuhn-2014, checked 2026-08-18 on a host with outbound network, verdict 'contradicts' against c-032. Every other claim_support verdict remains 'unchecked' and the investigation stays Silver. The session that opened it had no outbound network beyond server-side search: requests to the publishers, indexes, DOI resolvers and reference hosts were refused by the environment's egress policy, returning 403 from the proxy. Bibliographic metadata could therefore be confirmed from search results, and no source could be opened. Since a search summary can establish that a work exists but never what it argues, claim_support stays 'unchecked' throughout and this investigation stays Silver. Support is judged by meaning rather than by string equality (docs/source-audit.md §3a): equivalent wording supports a claim, and every substantive verdict must carry the source passage it rests on. Anyone completing it needs an environment that can reach the sources.

entries.cited_as: Kuhn 2014 survey of controlled natural languages, Computational Linguistics 40(1)

citation_accuracy.note: Tobias Kuhn, "A Survey and Classification of Controlled Natural Languages", Computational Linguistics 40(1):121-170, 2014. Venue, volume and issue match; the corpus does not state a page range, so none was checkable.

claim_support.quote: For type C, two studies on AECMA-SE showed that the use of controlled English significantly improves text comprehension, with a particularly large effect for complex texts and non-native speakers (Shubert et al. 1995; Chervak, Drury, and Ouellette 1996). The results of other studies were similar but not significant (Stewart 1998).
claim_support.note: Section 5.5 'Evaluations', page 145. The paper was opened and the section read in full. The worklist's premise was that Kuhn 2014 might be a pure classification survey carrying no outcome studies at all; it is not. Section 5.5 exists precisely to ask 'Do CNLs actually achieve the goals they were designed for?' and answers it with reported study results. This inverts the concern: the risk was that a load-bearing empirical claim rested on a survey that could not carry it, and instead the survey cuts against c-032. c-032 states that no strong empirical outcome studies showing STE improves comprehension were found in open sources. Kuhn 2014 is an open source this investigation already cites, and it names two such studies. AECMA-SE is STE under its former name: the same paper's appendix records that 'AECMA Simplified English (AECMA-SE) (AECMA 1986) was the predecessor of ASD Simplified Technical English.' What this does NOT settle is the word 'strong'. Kuhn reports findings, not designs, so whether Shubert et al. 1995 and Chervak, Drury and Ouellette 1996 meet the RCT bar c-032 names cannot be read off this survey. Settling that requires opening those two studies, which is the follow-up this entry generates. The correction published alongside c-032 states the verdict at exactly this strength and no further. See corrections.md, alongside this file.

citation_accuracy.note: A STEMG training document at this URL exists and is indexed. The host is unreachable from the auditing environment, so neither the document's date nor its issue could be established.

claim_support.note: Search results carry the same proposition in different words: the objective is simplified text for readers, and separately STE is not a simplified version of English for the writers. The corpus states that in one sentence. Under the same-meaning test that is equivalent wording, not a discrepancy, so the expected verdict is 'supports' with wording 'equivalent' once the primary document can be opened. Still unchecked only because no source could be read from the auditing environment. One thing to fix in the prose independently: the investigation prints this inside quotation marks, which asserts exact words, and it appears to compress two sentences into one.

entries.cited_as: Kincaid et al., 1975, readability formulas developed for the US Navy

claim_support.note: The load-bearing part is purpose, not existence: the claim is that the formulas were built to estimate difficulty of existing text for procurement, not to guide writing. That is the hinge of the Goodhart argument the whole series carries forward.
Supports the claim that STE removes devices persuasion depends on. Effect direction and size both matter here and neither is stated in the corpus.
